claims.text: In CrFeCoNiAl alloys, aluminum promotes segregation of Al at the metal–oxide interface during high-temperature exposure.
Interfacial aluminum reacts to form an Al-rich oxide, likely Al2O3.
The Al-rich oxide grows more slowly than the oxides formed on the Si- or Mn-containing variants.
The Al-rich oxide is continuous, coherent, and adherent.
The Al-rich oxide limits oxygen diffusion and ingress.
The Al-rich oxide mitigates stresses caused by thermal-expansion mismatch.
Limiting oxygen transport and thermal-mismatch stresses prevents rapid oxidation, cracking, and spallation.
CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn are less capable than CrFeCoNiAl of forming an adherent protective oxide.
Si- and Mn-containing variants form more heterogeneous and unstable oxide scales than the Al-containing variant.
Under identical exposure conditions, Si- and Mn-containing alloys will show faster oxide growth than the Al-containing alloy.
Under identical exposure conditions, Si- and Mn-containing alloys will show greater oxide porosity than the Al-containing alloy.
Under identical exposure conditions, Si- and Mn-containing alloys will show more cracking and spallation than the Al-containing alloy.
The comparison is intended to use homogeneous, single-phase CrFeCoNiX metallic solid solutions with X varied among Al, Si, and Mn.
The proposed hypothesis is limited to single-phase alloys and does not address multiphase alloys.
The proposed service boundary is an oxidative or corrosive environment at temperatures at or above 900 °C.

A controlled comparison at 950 °C using microscopy, compositional profiling, diffraction, and thermal cycling can distinguish oxide growth, chemistry, phase constitution, cracking, and spallation among the variants.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and intervention specify temperatures above 900 °C, whereas the conditions and boundary include exactly 900 °C by using ≥900 °C or 'at or above 900 °C'.
